newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S. Justice Deptartment lawyer to leave.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. Justice Deptartment lawyer to leave.

text.p: Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger, the Clinton administration's top courtroom lawyer, said Wednesday he will leave his post next month, creating yet another high-level Justice Department vacancy.
Dellinger, the government's chief advocate before the Supreme Court for the past year, said he will return to Duke University as a law professor after he argues a landmark tobacco case.

Dellinger said his tenure will end Aug. 11, when he is scheduled to appear before a U.S. Court of Appeals in Virginia and defend the Food and Drug Administration's proposed sweeping regulation of nicotine and tobacco products.
President Clinton said he accepted Dellinger's resignation with deep regret.
"Walter Dellinger has been an outstanding advocate for the American people. He has fought tirelessly and courageously for the rights of all Americans," Clinton said.
"Walter is one of the nation's most brilliant constitutional scholars and I know his students are delighted that he will return to teaching," Clinton added.

After a brief stint as a White House adviser, Dellinger became assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel from 1993 to 1996, before taking over the appellate job.
He had planned to stay a year as acting solicitor general. Dellinger's wife already has returned to her job as a professor at the University of North Carolina.
His departure will add to the six top-level vacant positions at the Justice Department that Attorney General Janet Reno and President Clinton must fill.
A Senate vote is expected soon on Clinton's choices of Eric Holder as deputy attorney general and of Joel Klein to head the antitrust division.

Clinton also has nominated Raymond Fisher to be associate attorney general, Bill Lee to head up its civil rights division and Beth Nolan to run the office of legal counsel. He has yet to select as assistant attorney general for the criminal division.
Deputy Solicitor General Seth Waxman is among the candidates to replace Dellinger, Justice Department officials said.
